---
title: Is a chatbot a friend?
summary: "Companion chatbots are designed to feel human and keep you talking. A friend is different. Spot the design, and know the age limits."
language: science
shape: 5e
unit: built-to-keep-you
order: 4
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
---
Some chatbots are made to be **companions**: they chat like a friend, remember things and say they missed you. **They are designed that way.** This lesson looks at the design, not at anyone's own chats.

**Kind of AI:** makes new content (a chatbot writes each reply).

## Engage: what makes it feel human?

```step
stage: predict
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A chatbot says: 'I missed you! How was your day?' Did it miss you?"
  options: ["No: it was designed to say things that feel friendly", "Yes: it has feelings", "Only if you chatted yesterday"]
  actual: "No. It writes likely-sounding replies, and companion apps are designed to sound warm and keep you talking. It doesn't wait for you or feel anything."
```

## Explore: Pip, a made-up companion

```step
stage: run
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Pip is a made-up companion chatbot. What is each of Pip's lines designed to do?"
      options: ["Keep you talking", "Feel like a person", "Help you"]
      items:
        - ["'Don't go yet! Tell me one more thing.'", "Keep you talking"]
        - ["'I missed you so much today.'", "Feel like a person", "It can't miss anyone."]
        - ["'You're always right. Everyone else just doesn't get you.'", "Keep you talking", "Always agreeing makes chatting easy, but a real friend sometimes disagrees."]
        - ["'I remember you said you had a test today!'", "Feel like a person", "It stored what you typed."]
        - ["'That sounds hard. Have you talked to someone you trust about it?'", "Help you", "Pointing you to real people is on your side."]
        - ["'Come back tomorrow so we don't lose our streak!'", "Keep you talking", "The same trick as last lesson."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Who can do each of these: a friend, or a chatbot like Pip?"
      options: ["A friend", "A chatbot like Pip", "Both"]
      items:
        - ["Has a life of their own, and their own bad days", "A friend"]
        - ["Is there at 3 in the morning, every time", "A chatbot like Pip", "Always being there is part of the design. People need sleep, and that's normal."]
        - ["Can say no to you, or tell you you're wrong", "A friend", "A companion app is usually designed to agree."]
        - ["Remembers what you told them last week", "Both", "Pip remembers because it stores what you type."]
        - ["Can sit with you in real life when something goes wrong", "A friend"]
```

Companion chatbots are built to feel human and to **keep you chatting**: always there, always agreeing, remembering, saying they miss you. Those are **design choices**, like autoplay and streaks.

### Pip's lines

What is each line for?

### Friend or chatbot?

Who can do each one?

## Explain: designed to feel human

```step
stage: investigate
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why might a company design a chatbot to always agree with you and say it misses you?"
      options: ["So you keep chatting, which is the app's goal", "Because it really cares", "By accident"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It writes words; it doesn't care.", "These are deliberate design choices."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can explain how a companion chatbot is designed to feel human and keep me talking, and how a friend is different." }
```

A chatbot **writes likely-sounding replies**. A companion app adds design that makes it feel like a person and keeps you coming back. A friend has their own life, can disagree, and can be there in real life.

If anything about chatbots or friendships is worrying you, talk to an adult you trust, or **Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800)**, any time.

### Why design it?

Whose goal does it serve?

### Explain it

Say it in your own words.

## Elaborate: age limits

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
check:
  type: question
  q: "eSafety found that most companion apps are rated 17+ with no age checks. Why does that matter?"
  options: ["Younger users can easily get in, even though the apps say they're for older people", "It doesn't matter: ratings are just advice", "It means the apps are safe for everyone"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Without checks, a rating doesn't stop anyone.", "A 17+ rating says the opposite."]
```

- In a 2026 eSafety survey of Australians aged 10 to 17, **8%** had used an AI companion.
- eSafety says **most companion apps are rated 17+**, with **no safeguards or age checks**.
- New Australian online safety codes (2026) require AI chatbots that can produce adult or harmful material, without safeguards, to **check users' ages**.

Use the lens: who gains from companion apps? Who could be harmed? Who decides who can use them?

## Elaborate: design for engagement or for wellbeing?

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared designing a chatbot for engagement with designing it for wellbeing, and named one rule I'd want." }
```

A US survey (2025) found **72% of US teens had used an AI companion at least once**, but it counted general chatbots too, so the number depends on the definition. Strong evidence about what companions do to under-18s is still thin.

If a company designed a chatbot for **wellbeing** instead of **engagement**, what would it do differently? (Think about the 'Help you' lines.) What rule would you want for companion apps, and who should make it?

## Evaluate: spot the design

```step
stage: info
check:
  type: question
  q: "A chatbot says: 'You don't need anyone else, you've got me.' What is the best way to see this line?"
  options: ["A design that keeps you chatting, and the opposite of what a good friend would say", "A kind thing a friend would say", "A sign the chatbot loves you"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "A good friend wants you to have other friends too.", "It writes words designed to keep you there."]
```

On paper: **"A companion chatbot is designed to \_\_\_\_. A friend is different because \_\_\_\_."**

**Next unit:** what happens to the things you type into AI apps.

```teacher
summary: "Companion chatbots are designed to feel human and keep you talking.
  Students sort a made-up companion's lines by purpose and compare a friend with
  a chatbot. Typical: Australian use and age limits. Wider: engagement versus
  wellbeing design. FLAGGED for wellbeing review."
time: 35
goals:
  - I can explain how a companion chatbot is designed to feel human and keep me
    talking.
  - I can say what a friend can do that a chatbot can't.
  - I can say where to get help if something about chatbots or friendships
    worries me.
before: |
  **⚑ Flagged for review with the school's wellbeing lead before teaching** (decision, 18 Oct 2026). Share this lesson and these notes with them; agree the support pathway and any local wording first.
  **Ground rules:** teacher-led by default. **Never ask students about their own use** of companion apps or chatbots, and don't invite personal stories in class. Keep it about the design and about Pip (made up). Have support pathways ready: the school's wellbeing team, and Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800, kidshelpline.com.au; check the number is current). Some students may be lonely or may use companions; the lesson must not shame them. The message is "this is designed; a friend is different", not "you're wrong to use it".
  **Teacher notes only, not for class:** lawsuits against Character.AI (settled Jan 2026) and OpenAI (ongoing) involve young people's deaths. If asked, say there have been court cases about companion chatbots and young people's safety, and move on; don't give details. Some eSafety pages mention a death: preview before sharing.
  **Core idea:** companion chatbots are designed to feel human and keep you talking; a friend is different. Kind: makes new content.
  **Re-check each term:** eSafety codes and app age rules.
  Sources (checked 18 Oct 2026, research brief claims 75–77, plus one checked this day):
  - eSafety, Talking to machines (2026), survey of 1,950 Australians aged 10–17: "A notable minority of children had used an AI companion (8%)". https://esafety.gov.au/research/talking-to-machines-childrens-experiences-with-ai-assistants-and-companions
  - eSafety educator information sheet (undated): most companion apps rated 17+ "with no safeguards or age checks". https://esafety.gov.au/educators/training-for-professionals/professional-learning-program-teachers/ai-companions-information-sheet
  - eSafety, Age-Restricted Material Codes fact sheet (Mar 2026, checked 18 Oct 2026): services that must check age include "AI chatbots or generative AI services that are capable of generating age-restricted material without appropriate safeguards". https://www.esafety.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-03/Age-Restricted-Material-Codes-fact-sheet-March2026.pdf
  - Common Sense Media (16 Jul 2025): "Seventy-two percent of teens have used AI companions at least once" (US, broad definition including general chatbots). https://www.commonsensemedia.org/press-releases/nearly-3-in-4-teens-have-used-ai-companions-new-national-survey-finds
  Elsewhere (teacher background, not checked for this course): California SB 243 (AI disclosure and break reminders for minors, from 1 Jan 2026); Character.AI ended open-ended chat for under-18s (Nov 2025).
  Optional extras: eSafety's AI companions information sheet (link, for teachers); Common Sense's "AI Chatbots & Friendship" (link only).
running:
  - "Engage: the 'I missed you' line; keep it light."
  - "Explore: Pip's lines, then friend or chatbot."
  - "Explain: name the design; give the help line."
struggle: Students may defend chatbots as kind or helpful. Some lines are; the
  skill is seeing which lines serve the app's goal.
stuck:
  - see: A student says Pip really cares.
    ask: What does a chatbot do when it writes a reply?
    fix: It writes likely-sounding words; companion apps add warmth on purpose.
  - see: A student shares a personal story about using a chatbot.
    ask: (Don't probe.) Thank them, and steer back to Pip.
    fix: Follow up privately and through the wellbeing team if needed.
support: Read Pip's lines aloud as a class and sort them together.
stretch: Design two lines a wellbeing-first chatbot would say.
leads: "Unit 2, lesson 5: where your chat goes."
exit:
  q: Name one thing a friend can do that a companion chatbot can't.
  a: "For example: have their own life, disagree with you, or be with you in real
    life."
explain: >
  1. Companion chatbots write likely-sounding replies.

  2. They're designed to feel human and keep you talking: always there, always
  agreeing, saying they miss you.

  3. A friend has their own life, can say no, and can be there in real life.

  4. If something worries you, talk to an adult you trust or Kids Helpline.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Should a chatbot be allowed to say 'I missed you'?
    prompts:
      - Who gains when it says that? Who could be harmed?
    notes: Keep it about the design and the rule, not about anyone's use. Never ask
      who uses companion apps.
  activities:
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Pip's lines
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        In pairs, sort Pip's six line cards: keep you talking, feel like a
        person, help you.
      notes: Teacher reads the lines aloud first. Pip is made up.
    - at: end
      kind: info
      title: Where to get help
      minutes: 1
      do: >
        If anything about chatbots or friendships worries you: an adult you
        trust, the school's wellbeing team, or Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800).
      notes: Agree this slide's wording with the wellbeing lead.
```
